mercy_translation.text:
If, without any sickness or pain, he had hidden the body away somewhere by himself—in a corner, a deserted place, a house, or wherever—and then suddenly appeared again and said that he had been raised from the dead, everyone would have thought he was telling stories. His claim about the resurrection would have been still less believed because there would have been no witness at all to his death. Death must precede resurrection; otherwise there is no resurrection. Therefore, if the death of the body had taken place secretly, with the death unseen and unwitnessed, the resurrection also would have been hidden and without testimony.

And why, after rising, would he proclaim the resurrection while making his death occur invisibly? Why did he drive out demons in the sight of all, give sight to the man blind from birth, and change water into wine so that through these works he might be believed to be the Word of God, yet not show the mortal body becoming incorruptible in the sight of all so that he might be believed to be Life itself?

How could his disciples have had boldness concerning the message of the resurrection if they could not say that he had first died? Or how could they be believed when saying that there had first been death and then resurrection unless the very people before whom they spoke had been witnesses of his death?

For if, even though both death and resurrection took place in the sight of all, the Pharisees of that time still refused to believe and even compelled those who had seen the resurrection to deny it, how many excuses for unbelief would they have invented if these things had happened secretly?

And how would the end of death and the victory over it have been shown unless, by calling death into the sight of all, he proved it dead—emptied of its power by the incorruption of the body?

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The public character of Christ's death is essential to Athanasius' apologetic for the resurrection.
The argument is historical and theological: death must be witnessed if resurrection is to be publicly proclaimed.
